en.title: English and Literary Studies: the whole course
en.short: What English and Literary Studies covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: English and Literary Studies is the university study of the English language and of literature written in English, including African literature. It joins two questions. How does English work as a language: its sounds, grammar, vocabulary, meaning, history and social uses? What does imaginative writing do: how poems, plays, novels and oral forms create meaning and respond to their societies? The degree trains close reading, clear writing, linguistic analysis and research. Graduates teach, write, edit, publish, work in media, law, public service or continue to postgraduate study. It is not only the reading of novels; it is a discipline with methods and evidence.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text: Awards and lengths differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria the common award is a BA in English, English Language and Literature, or English and Literary Studies. A full-time BA commonly takes four years, with foundation courses, core literature and language courses, electives and a final long essay. The National Universities Commission (NUC) sets minimum academic standards for Nigerian universities. Some programmes are combined honours with another subject. In the United Kingdom a BA English is commonly three years full time; in the United States a BA in English is commonly four years. Ghana and Kenya also offer BA English programmes, but structures vary. Master’s degrees usually take one to two years and include coursework and a dissertation. Always confirm duration, credit loads and graduation requirements with your department.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The early stage builds foundations. You begin with what English studies is, then the sounds of English in phonetics and phonology, grammar of words, phrases and clauses, and lexis and semantics. You study the history of English and the spread of African and world Englishes. Introduction to Literature teaches literary appreciation; oral literature in Africa shows that verbal art exists beyond the written page; foundations of criticism introduce ways of reading.

The core stage moves through genres and traditions. Poetry, prose fiction and drama each have their own forms, and drama adds performance. You study African literature in English and Nigerian literature, then English literature from Shakespeare and the seventeenth century through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries to the twentieth century and after. Literary theory and comparative literature deepen analysis. Language courses cover first and second language acquisition, sociolinguistics, pragmatics and discourse analysis, stylistics, and composition and rhetoric. Literature and society examines politics, gender and the environment. Research methods prepares the long essay.

At master’s level you may take advanced literary theory, advanced English linguistics and corpus methods, research design for the dissertation, and frontier areas such as digital humanities and global Anglophone studies.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read primary texts before secondary criticism. For a novel, note narrator, plot, character, setting, language and context. For a poem, read aloud and mark sound, line breaks and images. For a play, imagine staging and performance.

Keep a language notebook. For each term, write a definition in your own words and one example from real speech or a text. Practise transcription for phonetics and tree or phrase analysis for grammar only as your course requires. Build a timeline of English literature and history, but do not memorise dates without a text or event attached.

Write regularly and get feedback. Summarise an article in one paragraph, then criticise it. Use the library and reliable databases. For the long essay, choose a narrow question, keep a record of sources and follow your department’s citation style.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is to retell a story instead of analysing how it works. Another is to use theory as a label without showing what it reveals in the text. Students also quote critics without checking the original or without page references.

In language work, many confuse letters with sounds, or describe English as if it were the same everywhere. English has many varieties, and Nigerian English is one. Do not present one country’s examination system, spelling rule or literary canon as universal.

In research, weak essays often ask a question too broad to answer. Others use a sample or text that cannot support the claim. Plagiarism is a serious risk, so keep notes with sources. Check your handbook for rules on deadlines, word limits and referencing.

keyPoints: English and Literary Studies joins the study of the English language with the study of literature written in English, including African literature.
Degree titles, lengths and credit rules differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Study literature by analysing how texts work, not by retelling their plots.
English has many varieties, and African Englishes are legitimate objects of study.
Language courses train description and evidence, not only opinions about correctness.
Research and the long essay need a narrow question, reliable sources and correct referencing.

en.title: English and Literary Studies: What the Field Is
en.short: How language study and literature in English form one degree, its history, parts and careers.

sections.heading: One field, two sides
sections.text:
English and Literary Studies is a degree that studies the English language and literature written in English. The two sides are joined. Language study asks how English is built and used: its grammar, sounds, word meanings, history, varieties and social roles. Literature study asks what imaginative writing means and how it works. The literature is not only from England. It includes African literature in English and writing from many countries.

A simple case shows the link. A class may take one passage from a novel and ask two questions: how are the sentences built, and what does the passage mean in its setting? The first question belongs to language study; the second to literary study. Good work often uses both.

sections.heading: How it grew
sections.text: The field grew from older subjects. Philology is the historical study of language and texts. It compared languages, traced word forms and edited old manuscripts. Literary criticism is the interpretation and judgement of writing. It asks what a text means, how it achieves its effects and whether it is good. In universities these subjects were once separate. Over time they came together in degree programmes that train students to read language and literature together. The exact history differs by country and university.

sections.heading: Main parts
sections.text: The main parts are language, literature, criticism and research. Language covers grammar, phonetics, meaning, history and varieties. Literature covers poetry, prose fiction and drama, including African writing. Criticism and theory examine assumptions behind reading and judgement. Research methods and academic writing teach students to find sources, form arguments and present evidence. These parts support one another rather than compete.

sections.heading: Where graduates work
sections.text: Graduates enter teaching, publishing, editing, journalism, media, public relations, advertising, civil service and non-governmental work. Some go on to law, library science, communication or postgraduate research; these usually need further study. Exact job markets and requirements vary by country. The degree trains careful reading, clear writing and reasoned argument, which many employers value.

keyPoints: English and Literary Studies joins the study of the English language with literature written in English, including African literature.
The field grew from philology, the historical study of language and texts, and literary criticism, the interpretation and judgement of writing.
Its language side studies grammar, sounds, meaning, history, varieties and use; its literature side studies poetry, prose and drama.
Criticism and theory ask how texts mean and how readers judge them, while research and academic writing hold the degree together.
Graduates enter teaching, publishing, media, public relations, civil service, law and further research, depending on training and country.
Programme titles and requirements differ by country and university, so check the current handbook.

en.title: Sounds of English: Phonetics and Phonology
en.short: How English speech sounds are made, classified and patterned, with RP, GA and African accents.

sections.heading: Making speech sounds
sections.text:
Phonetics studies speech sounds as physical events. Most English sounds use a pulmonic egressive airstream: air is pushed from the lungs. Active articulators include the lower lip and tongue parts: tip, blade, front and back. Passive places include the upper teeth, alveolar ridge, hard palate and soft palate.

A consonant is classified by place, manner (stop, fricative, nasal) and voicing. The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) chart arranges symbols by these features. Vowels are classified by tongue height, backness and lip rounding.

sections.heading: Phonemes and syllables
sections.text:
Phonology studies how sounds pattern in a language. A phoneme is a contrastive sound unit. In English /p/ and /b/ are phonemes because pin and bin differ. An allophone is a variant of one phoneme that does not change meaning.

English /p/ is aspirated [pʰ] at the start of pin but unaspirated [p] after s in spin; the difference is allophonic. A syllable has a nucleus, usually a vowel, with optional onset and coda. In cat, /k/ is onset, /æ/ nucleus, /t/ coda. English allows clusters, as in strengths.

sections.heading: Stress and intonation
sections.text:
Stress is the prominence given to a syllable through loudness, length and pitch. English has word stress, as in REcord (noun) and reCORD (verb), and sentence stress, which highlights important words.

Intonation is the pitch pattern over a phrase. A falling tone often marks a statement; a rising tone can mark a yes-no question or continuation. These are tendencies, not fixed rules.

sections.heading: Accents compared
sections.text:
Received Pronunciation (RP) is a non-rhotic accent of England: r is pronounced only before a vowel, so car is /kɑː/. General American (GA) is a rhotic accent of the United States: car is /kɑːr/. RP and GA also differ in vowels, as in BATH and LOT.

Nigerian English is not one accent. Educated Nigerian English often has fewer vowel contrasts, less reduction of unstressed vowels and a more even rhythm than RP or GA. Ghanaian, Kenyan and South African English differ too. No accent is superior.

keyPoints: Phonetics studies physical speech sounds; phonology studies how sounds pattern in a language.
Consonants are classified by place, manner and voicing; vowels by height, backness and rounding.
A phoneme contrasts meanings, while an allophone is a non-contrastive variant.
A syllable has a nucleus and optional onset and coda, and English permits consonant clusters.
Stress gives prominence to syllables, and intonation is the pitch pattern across a phrase.
RP is non-rhotic and GA is rhotic, while Nigerian and other African English accents vary and are not inferior.

en.title: English Grammar: Words, Phrases and Clauses
en.short: Parts of speech, phrases, clauses, sentence patterns, tree diagrams, tense, aspect, mood and agreement.

sections.heading: Words and word classes
sections.text: Words fall into word classes, also called parts of speech. The main ones are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and determiner. A word’s class depends on its work in a sentence, not only on its form. In “The old man walks slowly”, the is a determiner, old an adjective, man a noun, walks a verb and slowly an adverb. Traditional grammars count eight classes, with interjection in place of determiner; in modern grammar, articles belong to the determiner class.

sections.heading: Phrases and rules
sections.text: A phrase is a group of words that acts as one unit and has no subject-predicate pair. A noun phrase may be just a noun, or a determiner with modifiers: “the small market”. A verb phrase contains the main verb and any auxiliaries: “has been waiting”. Phrase structure rules show how units combine. For example, S = NP + VP means a sentence consists of a noun phrase and a verb phrase. A tree diagram draws this: S branches to NP and VP; NP branches to Det and N; VP branches to V and Adv. In “The child sleeps quietly”, the tree separates the subject noun phrase from the predicate verb phrase.

sections.heading: Clauses and patterns
sections.text: A clause contains a subject and a predicate. An independent clause can stand alone; a dependent clause cannot. Basic English sentence patterns include subject + verb (“Birds sing”), subject + verb + object (“She reads novels”), subject + verb + complement (“He is a teacher”) and subject + verb + object + object (“They gave her a book”). Word order matters: “The dog bit the man” differs from “The man bit the dog”.

sections.heading: Tense and agreement
sections.text: Tense locates time: present “works”, past “worked”. Aspect shows how an action is viewed: progressive “is working”, perfect “has worked”. Mood shows the speaker’s attitude: indicative states facts, imperative commands, subjunctive expresses wishes or unreal conditions. Agreement means the verb matches its subject: “The boy runs”, “The boys run”. Standard written English uses fixed word order, usually subject before verb.

keyPoints: Word class depends on a word’s function in the sentence.
A phrase is a unit without a subject-predicate pair; a clause has one.
The rule S = NP + VP is the basic sentence rule, and tree diagrams show its parts.
Basic patterns include SV, SVO, SVC and SVOO.
Tense shows time, aspect shows how action is viewed, and mood shows attitude.
Subject-verb agreement and fixed word order are central to standard written English.

en.title: Words and Meaning: Lexis and Semantics
en.short: How English words are formed and how word meanings relate, including sense relations and figurative language.

sections.heading: Lexis and word formation
sections.text: Lexis is the vocabulary of a language; a lexeme is a word or fixed expression stored as one unit. New lexemes come from word formation. Affixation adds a bound morpheme, an affix, to a base: un- + happy gives unhappy, and happy + -ness gives happiness. Compounding joins two free morphemes, words that can stand alone, as in bedroom or blackboard. Blending fuses parts of two words, as in breakfast + lunch = brunch. Clipping shortens a word without changing its core meaning, as in advertisement to ad or gymnasium to gym. Conversion changes a word’s word class without adding an affix, as when the noun email becomes the verb to email.

sections.heading: Sense relations
sections.text: Semantics studies meaning, especially sense, the meaning a word has within the language system. Synonymy is sameness or near-sameness of sense: begin and start. True synonyms are rare because register and collocation differ. Antonymy is oppositeness: hot and cold are gradable, while dead and alive are complementary. Hyponymy is inclusion: rose is a hyponym of flower, and flower is its superordinate. Polysemy is one lexeme with several related senses, as head of a person and head of a department. Homonymy, by contrast, is unrelated senses that happen to share a form, as bank of a river and bank for money.

sections.heading: Literal and figurative
sections.text: Literal meaning is the conventional, direct sense of an expression. Figurative meaning extends it through comparison or association: “The market is a jungle” does not describe plants but competition. Metaphor, simile and idiom depend on this extension. Context usually decides which sense is active.

sections.heading: Accounts of sense
sections.text: Componential analysis breaks a word’s sense into features, for example man as [+human, +adult, +male]. Structural accounts treat sense as a network of relations, so the meaning of uncle depends on its links to parent and male. Both accounts are useful, but neither captures every shade of meaning.

keyPoints: Lexis is vocabulary; a lexeme is a stored word or fixed expression.
Affixation adds bound morphemes, compounding joins free morphemes, blending fuses parts, clipping shortens, and conversion changes word class.
Synonymy is near-sameness, antonymy is oppositeness, hyponymy is inclusion, and polysemy is one form with related senses.
Literal meaning is direct; figurative meaning extends sense through comparison or association.
Componential analysis uses semantic features, while structural accounts describe sense through relations.

en.title: The History of the English Language
en.short: Old English to Modern English: Norse and French contact, printing, and the spread of English to West Africa.

sections.heading: Old English, 450 to 1100
sections.text:
Germanic settlers, the Angles, Saxons and Jutes, brought their dialects to Britain from the fifth century. Their speech, Old English, was heavily inflected: nouns and adjectives changed endings for case and gender, and word order was freer than today. Its vocabulary was mostly Germanic, with Latin added after the Christian mission of 597. Beowulf is its best-known poem.

From 793 Norse raiders, and later settlers in the Danelaw, brought Old Norse. Because the two languages were close, they mixed easily. English gained everyday words such as sky, egg, knife, take and they, and its endings began to wear away.

sections.heading: Middle English and French
sections.text:
After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French became the language of court, law and administration for about three centuries, while English remained the speech of most people. Middle English, roughly 1100 to 1500, borrowed heavily from French: government, justice, parliament, court, marriage. Most inflectional endings were lost, so word order carried more meaning.

By the late fourteenth century English was returning to official use, and Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in it. The Great Vowel Shift, a change in the sound of long vowels between about 1400 and 1700, helps explain why English spelling no longer matches pronunciation.

sections.heading: Printing and Early Modern English
sections.text: William Caxton set up the first printing press in England at Westminster in 1476. Printing fixed spellings and spread one written standard. Early Modern English, roughly 1500 to 1700, borrowed thousands of words from Latin and Greek. Shakespeare wrote in this period, and the King James Bible appeared in 1611.

sections.heading: English goes global
sections.text:
British trade, settlement and empire, and later American power, carried English around the world. In West Africa it arrived with European traders from the sixteenth century and spread through British mission schools in the nineteenth.

In Nigeria, English is the official language and medium of instruction, but a second language for most people, alongside hundreds of local languages. Contact produced Nigerian Pidgin and West African Englishes.

keyPoints: Old English was a heavily inflected Germanic language; Norse contact wore down its endings and added everyday words.
After 1066 French supplied law, government and court vocabulary, and Middle English lost most inflectional endings.
Caxton’s press of 1476 helped fix spelling, and the Great Vowel Shift explains many gaps between spelling and sound.
Early Modern English borrowed heavily from Latin and Greek.
English spread through trade, empire and later American influence; in West Africa it came with coastal trade and mission schools.
In Nigeria English is official and the medium of instruction, but a second language for most people, and contact produced Pidgin and West African Englishes.

en.title: African Englishes and World Englishes
en.short: Kachru’s circles, the spread of English, Nigerian English features, and the standard-variety debate.

sections.heading: Models and spread
sections.text:
World Englishes means the many varieties of English. Kachru’s Three Circles model (1985) groups them by history and use. The Inner Circle covers first-language countries such as Britain and the United States. The Outer Circle covers postcolonial countries where English is official or a second language, such as Nigeria, Ghana, India and Kenya. The Expanding Circle covers countries where English is mainly foreign, such as Japan and Brazil. The model is useful but simplified. Schneider’s Dynamic Model (2007) describes postcolonial Englishes developing through stages, from foundation to differentiation.

English spread through British colonial rule, trade, migration, science, technology, American power and the internet. It is a global lingua franca, a shared language between people who do not share a first language. Speakers adapt it, so local varieties develop.

sections.heading: Nigerian English features
sections.text:
West African English, including Nigerian English, is not one uniform accent. In sound, many speakers use syllable-timed rhythm, simplify final consonant clusters, and replace /θ/ and /ð/ with /t/ and /d/ or similar sounds. Stress may differ from British English.

In vocabulary, English words gain local meanings, and Nigerian coinages and words from Nigerian languages enter English, for example okada for a motorcycle taxi. In grammar, some speakers use general question tags such as isn’t it? and pluralise some mass nouns. Usage varies by region, education and setting, so these are tendencies, not rules for every speaker.

sections.heading: Standard and codification
sections.text:
A standard variety is the accepted norm for education, publishing and public life. The debate asks whether Nigerian English should follow British English, an outside or exonormative norm, or develop a local or endonormative norm based on educated Nigerian usage. Supporters of a Nigerian standard cite identity and local intelligibility. Critics cite international intelligibility and examination expectations.

Codification means recording a variety in dictionaries, grammars, spelling rules and usage guides. Nigerian scholars have produced dictionaries and descriptions, but no single standard is fully settled. Check current official and scholarly sources.

keyPoints: Kachru’s Three Circles model divides English into Inner, Outer and Expanding Circles by history and use.
English became global through colonial expansion, trade, technology and media, and it serves as a lingua franca.
West African and Nigerian English features include syllable-timed rhythm, simplified final clusters, and /θ/ and /ð/ often replaced by /t/ and /d/ or similar.
Nigerian English vocabulary includes local coinages and loanwords such as okada, and grammar shows tendencies such as general question tags.
The standard-variety debate opposes exonormative British norms and an endonormative Nigerian standard.
Codification records a variety in dictionaries and grammars, but no single Nigerian standard is fully settled.

en.title: Introduction to Literature and Literary Appreciation
en.short: What literature is, its main genres, basic reading skills and how to write a short appreciation.

sections.heading: What literature is
sections.text: Literature is imaginative writing that uses language in patterned, suggestive ways to explore human experience. It is not simply any written text. In African literary studies it also includes oral forms such as folktales and praise poetry. The three main genres are poetry, prose fiction and drama. Poetry compresses language into lines, often with rhythm and imagery. Prose fiction tells a story in sentences and paragraphs, usually through a narrator. Drama is written for performance, so dialogue and action carry the meaning. Genres can mix, but these are the basic divisions.

sections.heading: Reading skills
sections.text: To read closely, ask six questions. Theme is the central idea or question the text explores, such as duty or loss. Plot is the sequence of events linked by cause and effect, not just a list. Character is a person in the story, shown by speech, action and description. Setting is the time and place, which can shape mood and meaning. Point of view is who tells the story: first person (I), third person limited (one character’s view) or omniscient (all-knowing). Tone is the speaker’s attitude, for example calm, bitter or amused. Quote short evidence for each claim.

sections.heading: Writing appreciation
sections.text: To write an appreciation, state the text, then give a one-sentence summary. Discuss two or three features, using evidence. For example, take an invented couplet: 'The harmattan dust settles on the mango leaves; / Mama sweeps the step again.' The theme is endurance in daily life. The setting is a dusty harmattan morning. The tone is quiet and respectful. The image of repeated sweeping suggests persistence. End by linking these features to the theme. Keep your view balanced and support it with words from the text.

keyPoints: Literature is imaginative composition, spoken or written, that uses language in patterned ways to explore experience.
The three main genres are poetry, prose fiction and drama.
Theme, plot, character, setting, point of view and tone are basic tools of close reading.
Point of view is who tells the story; tone is the speaker’s attitude.
A short appreciation states the text, summarises it, discusses features with evidence and links them to theme.

en.title: Oral Literature in Africa: Genres, Performance and Collection
en.short: African oral genres, their performance and social roles, and how orature is collected and written.

sections.heading: Genres of orature
sections.text: Oral literature, or orature, is spoken or sung art passed on by performance rather than only by writing. Its main genres overlap. Oral poetry is verse recited or sung, often with rhythm and repetition. Folktales are narrative stories, often with animal tricksters. Proverbs are short, fixed sayings that carry shared wisdom. Riddles are puzzles with conventional answers, often used in games. Praise poetry names and celebrates a person, family, animal or place. An oral epic is a long heroic narrative performed over time, often with music.

sections.heading: Performance and function
sections.text: Oral genres exist in performance: a singer, storyteller or reciter performs before an audience. Call-and-response, where the performer calls and the audience answers, is part of the work, as are gesture, music and audience reaction. The context shapes meaning. A praise poem at a wedding honours lineage and strengthens family ties; a folktale told to children teaches conduct and warns of danger; proverbs settle disputes or give advice, and elders often use them; riddles sharpen memory and language. Oral literature also stores history, law and belief. For example, a praise singer at a naming ceremony may recite the child’s family line, and the audience answers to confirm shared memory.

sections.heading: Collecting and writing
sections.text: Collectors record performances, then transcribe (write down) and translate them. Transcription is interpretation: tone, gesture, pauses and audience response are hard to put on paper. Fieldworkers need consent, fair credit and care with sacred or private material. Archives and editions make oral texts available, but they freeze one version of a living art. Written African literature often draws on orature: writers adapt folktales, proverbs and praise forms. The relation is not simply oral to written; the two continue side by side and influence each other.

keyPoints: Oral literature, or orature, is performed art, so the text on paper is only one part of it.
The main genres are oral poetry, folktales, proverbs, riddles, praise poetry and oral epic.
Performance context, including audience, music and gesture, shapes meaning and social function.
Oral genres teach conduct, store history, settle disputes, honour people and entertain.
Collection involves recording, transcription, translation, consent and fair credit.
Written African literature often adapts oral forms, and oral and written traditions continue side by side.

en.title: Approaches to Literary Criticism: The Foundations
en.short: Formalism, New Criticism, close reading, moral criticism and reader-response views.

sections.heading: Formalism and New Criticism
sections.text: Formalism treats a literary work as a verbal object. It studies language, structure and devices rather than the author’s life or social history. Russian Formalism arose in the early twentieth century; the New Criticism was an Anglo-American movement that dominated mid-century teaching. New Critics read closely and warned against the intentional fallacy, judging a work by what the author meant, and the affective fallacy, judging it by a reader’s emotions. Criticism, they argued, should begin with the words on the page.

sections.heading: Tools of close reading
sections.text: Close reading examines short passages. Imagery is descriptive language that appeals to the senses. Irony is a gap between what is said and what is meant, or between expectation and outcome. Ambiguity is a word or passage open to more than one meaning. Paradox is a seeming contradiction that may reveal a truth; tension is the strain between opposing ideas. In the invented line “The flag stood stiff in the rain”, “stiff” may suggest dignity or rigidity, an ambiguity; if the flag is honoured while the rain suggests grief, the effect is ironic. Close reading links such details to the whole.

sections.heading: Moral and didactic views
sections.text: Moral criticism asks what literature does to character. The didactic view, from Greek didasko, to teach, judges a work by its moral lesson: it should instruct and delight. Plato worried that poetry could weaken reason; later defenders argued that good literature shapes virtue. This approach can illuminate ethical questions, but it risks reducing a complex work to a simple message and ignoring its form.

sections.heading: Reader-response views
sections.text: Reader-response criticism holds that meaning is made in the act of reading, not simply found in the text. Readers bring expectations, memories and social positions. Stanley Fish argued that members of an interpretive community share ways of reading, so their interpretations are not merely private. This view explains why responses differ, but it can underplay the text’s power to correct a reader. Many critics combine it with close reading.

keyPoints: Formalism and New Criticism focus on the text’s language and form, not author biography or social history.
Close reading analyses imagery, irony, ambiguity, paradox and tension in short passages.
New Criticism warns against the intentional fallacy and the affective fallacy.
Moral or didactic criticism judges literature by its ethical teaching and can reduce art to a message.
Reader-response criticism says meaning is made by readers, often within interpretive communities.
No single approach is final, and critics often combine close reading with other questions.

en.title: Poetry: Form, Sound and Language
en.short: Metre, rhyme, stanza, free verse, sound patterns and the poetic line in lyric, narrative and dramatic poetry.

sections.heading: Metre and the line
sections.text:
Metre is the regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line. A foot is one unit of that pattern; an iamb is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one. Five iambs make iambic pentameter. Scansion marks stresses and divides feet. Read aloud first, then mark natural stresses.

Shakespeare’s Sonnet 18 opens: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?' It scans as shall I | comPARE | thee TO | a SUM | mer’s DAY, five iambs. The line is end-stopped, ending with punctuation. Enjambment runs the sentence past the line break, creating speed or suspense. Line breaks and pauses shape meaning as much as metre.

sections.heading: Rhyme, stanza, sound
sections.text:
Rhyme is the repetition of similar sounds, usually at line ends. End rhyme, internal rhyme and slant rhyme (near rhyme) create echoes. A rhyme scheme is the pattern, written abab or abba. A stanza is a group of lines; a couplet is two lines, a quatrain four. A sonnet is fourteen lines, but its form varies.

Sound patterns include alliteration (repeated consonants at word starts), assonance (repeated vowel sounds) and consonance (repeated consonant sounds within or at the ends of words). Onomatopoeia imitates sound. These patterns can make a poem musical, or underline an image or mood. Ask what they do, not only what they are.

sections.heading: Forms and close reading
sections.text:
Lyric poetry is short and songlike, often expressing one speaker’s thought or feeling. Narrative poetry tells a story, as in the ballad or epic. Dramatic poetry presents a character speaking; the dramatic monologue is a type. African poets such as Wole Soyinka, Christopher Okigbo, Gabriel Okara, Niyi Osundare and Tanure Ojaide often draw on oral praise, drum rhythm and local English. Read them for form and context.

Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme, but it is not formless. It uses line breaks, repetition, spacing and speech rhythm. Explication means explaining a short poem line by line. Read aloud, identify speaker and tone, scan a few lines, note rhyme and stanza shape, then link each formal choice to meaning.

keyPoints: Metre is patterned stress; an iamb is unstressed then stressed, and five iambs make iambic pentameter.
A rhyme scheme is the pattern of end rhymes, and stanza forms such as the couplet and quatrain shape a poem’s movement.
Alliteration, assonance and consonance create emphasis, music and mood.
Free verse lacks fixed metre and rhyme but uses line breaks, repetition and speech rhythm.
Lyric, narrative and dramatic poetry differ in speaker, purpose and story.
Scansion and explication connect formal choices to meaning; read aloud and mark stresses carefully.

en.title: Prose Fiction: Narrative and the Novel
en.short: Plot, character, setting, theme, narrator, focalisation, narrative time, and novel versus short story.

sections.heading: Narrative building blocks
sections.text: Plot is the causal arrangement of events, not just a list. Characterisation is how a writer builds persons: direct description, action, speech and what others say. Setting is place, time and social world. Theme is a recurring idea, not a simple moral, such as change and resistance. In Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958), Okonkwo’s rise and fall in Umuofia are plotted against the arrival of colonial rule. The setting carries history: clan law, farming seasons, missionaries and the district court are not background but pressures on character.

sections.heading: Voice and time
sections.text: The narrator is the voice that tells. Focalisation is the perspective through which we perceive events. A third-person narrator may be omniscient or limited to one character’s knowledge. Narrative time concerns order (flashback or flash-forward), duration (summary or scene) and frequency (what is told once or repeatedly). Things Fall Apart uses a mostly external, omniscient narrator who stays close to Okonkwo, then shifts at the end to the District Commissioner’s viewpoint. That shift turns a personal tragedy into a colonial record, showing how form carries social change.

sections.heading: Novel and short story
sections.text: The novel is a long prose fiction, usually with several characters, places and plotlines, and room for developed setting and social history. The short story is shorter and often built around a single incident, a turning point or a single effect. These are tendencies, not fixed rules. Length alone does not define genre; scope and compression matter. A novel can be short and a long story can be complex. Read form as meaning: in African novels, the scale of the novel can hold family, community and colonial change together.

keyPoints: Plot is the causal arrangement of events, while characterisation, setting and theme are separate narrative elements.
The narrator is the telling voice; focalisation is the perspective through which events are perceived.
Narrative time includes order, duration and frequency, such as flashback, summary and repeated telling.
Achebe’s Things Fall Apart shows how a shift in viewpoint can turn personal tragedy into colonial history.
The novel usually offers greater scope and multiple plotlines than the short story, but the boundary is flexible.
Read narrative form as meaning, because African novels use structure to carry history and social change.

en.title: Drama and Theatre: Text and Performance
en.short: Dramatic structure, conflict, dialogue, stage directions, genres, text versus performance, and Nigerian theatre.

sections.heading: Structure and conflict
sections.text:
Dramatic structure is the arrangement of events in a play. A common pattern is exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Exposition gives background; rising action builds complications; the climax is the turning point; the resolution settles the outcome. Modern drama may use open or closed forms.

Conflict is the opposition that drives action. It may set a character against another person, society, nature, fate, or himself or herself. Conflict need not be loud; a quiet refusal can be dramatic. The audience’s knowledge of what a character does not know can create tension.

sections.heading: Dialogue and directions
sections.text: Dialogue is speech exchanged by characters. In performance it carries tone, pace and silence. Good dramatic dialogue does several jobs: it reveals character, advances plot and creates subtext, meaning what is implied rather than said. Stage directions are the playwright’s instructions in the script. They describe setting, entrances, movement, gesture, lighting, sound and tone. Some directors follow them closely; others interpret them.

sections.heading: Tragedy, comedy, tragicomedy
sections.text: Tragedy presents serious action and suffering, often ending in death or loss. Aristotle described tragedy as arousing pity and fear and effecting catharsis, an emotional purging; later writers vary the pattern. Comedy aims to amuse and often ends in reconciliation, marriage or a restored society, while exposing folly. Tragicomedy mixes tragic and comic elements; it may refuse a neat happy or sad ending.

sections.heading: Text, performance, Africa
sections.text:
A play as text is a script; as performance it is an event shaped by actors, director, space, costume, music and audience. Each production interprets it.

African theatre includes festival, masquerade and oral performance. Yoruba travelling theatre toured western Nigeria from the 1940s, combining music, dance and drama in companies led by Hubert Ogunde, Kola Ogunmola and Duro Ladipo. Wole Soyinka and J.P. Clark have written for page and stage. Soyinka’s Death and the King’s Horseman uses drumming, dance and ritual; its stage directions show how performance completes meaning. Clark’s Song of a Goat sets a communal tragedy in the Niger Delta.

keyPoints: Dramatic structure usually moves through exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution, though plays may vary.
Conflict is the opposition of forces that drives dramatic action.
Dialogue reveals character and advances plot, while stage directions guide performance.
Tragedy treats serious suffering, comedy exposes folly and seeks reconciliation, and tragicomedy mixes both.
A play is both a script and a performance shaped by actors, space, music and audience.
Yoruba travelling theatre and writers such as Soyinka and Clark show Nigerian drama’s roots in ritual, music and communal performance.

en.title: African Literature in English
en.short: Growth of modern African writing in English, key novels and plays, and the language and audience debates.

sections.heading: Beginnings and Negritude
sections.text:
Modern African writing in English grew from the 1950s. Amos Tutuola’s The Palm-Wine Drinkard (1952) drew on Yoruba oral tale; Cyprian Ekwensi’s People of the City (1954) pictured city life. Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) became a model: a narrative of Igbo society before and after colonial contact, using proverbs and English.

Negritude was a French-language movement of the 1930s, linked to Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas. It affirmed black culture against colonial racism. Some anglophone writers, including Wole Soyinka, were sceptical of its racial rhetoric. African literature also exists in other languages; this summary follows English.

sections.heading: Independence and women
sections.text:
The first generation wrote around independence. Achebe’s A Man of the People (1966) turned to corruption. Ngugi wa Thiong’o's Weep Not, Child (1964) and A Grain of Wheat (1967) examine Kenyan land, education and the Mau Mau struggle. Soyinka’s plays, including A Dance of the Forests (1960) and Death and the King’s Horseman (1975), mix Yoruba ritual, satire and poetry.

Postcolonial writing examines colonial rule and its aftermath. After independence, disillusion, coups and civil war produced a darker generation; Ngugi’s Petals of Blood (1977) attacks neocolonial exploitation. Buchi Emecheta’s Second Class Citizen (1974) follows a Nigerian woman in London, and The Joys of Motherhood (1979) questions motherhood.

sections.heading: Language and audience
sections.text:
Achebe argued that English could be adapted to carry African experience, creating a new voice. Ngugi wa Thiong’o rejected English for creative work, most fully in Decolonising the Mind (1986), and wrote in Gikuyu, with translations. He held that language carries colonial power and that writers should reach ordinary people in their own languages. Achebe replied that a shared language can reach wider audiences.

The audience debate asks: is African literature written for local readers, for the nation, or for the world? Oral forms, translation and publishing shape the answer. There is no settled resolution.

keyPoints: Modern African writing in English emerged in the 1950s, with Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) as a landmark.
Negritude was a French-language movement affirming black culture; anglophone writers such as Soyinka were sometimes sceptical.
Post-independence writing often turned from hope to disillusion, corruption and neocolonial exploitation.
Emecheta and other women writers centre gender, motherhood, migration and patriarchy.
Achebe defended adapting English; Ngugi rejected it for creative work and wrote in Gikuyu.
The audience debate asks whether African literature is for local, national or international readers, and it remains unsettled.

en.title: Nigerian Literature: Writers and Movements
en.short: Onitsha market pamphlets, Mbari, Heinemann, Achebe, Soyinka, Clark, Okigbo, Adichie and Habila.

sections.heading: Onitsha market literature
sections.text: Onitsha market literature is the name for cheap pamphlets sold in Onitsha market from the 1940s to the 1960s. They included romances, moral tales, plays and advice books, written in accessible English and local idiom for a new reading public. Cyprian Ekwensi is often linked to this popular tradition. The pamphlets show that Nigerian writing in English began with popular as well as elite audiences.

sections.heading: Mbari and Heinemann
sections.text: The Mbari Club, founded in Ibadan in 1961, was a meeting place and publisher for writers and artists. Its members and guests included Achebe, Soyinka, Clark and Okigbo. In 1962 Heinemann launched the African Writers Series, with Achebe as founding editor. The series reprinted established titles and published new African writing in affordable editions, helping Nigerian literature travel beyond Nigeria.

sections.heading: Major writers
sections.text: Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) is a founding novel of modern African literature; it portrays Igbo life and the arrival of colonial rule. Wole Soyinka, Nobel laureate in 1986, is known for plays such as Death and the King’s Horseman, as well as poetry and fiction. John Pepper Clark is a poet and playwright; Christopher Okigbo is a major poet whose work appeared in the 1960s before his death in the Nigerian Civil War. Their writing often draws on oral tradition and history.

sections.heading: Contemporary writing
sections.text: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s novels, including Purple Hibiscus (2003) and Half of a Yellow Sun (2006), explore family, war and diaspora. Helon Habila’s Waiting for an Angel (2002) and Oil on Water (2010) treat dictatorship and oil politics. Contemporary poetry includes Niyi Osundare’s public, oral-inflected verse and younger poets in print and online. Publishers, prizes and digital media now shape a more global Nigerian literature.

keyPoints: Onitsha market literature was popular pamphlet writing sold in Onitsha from the 1940s to the 1960s.
The Mbari Club in Ibadan, founded in 1961, brought writers and artists together and published their work.
Heinemann’s African Writers Series, launched in 1962 with Achebe as editor, made African writing widely available.
Achebe, Soyinka, Clark and Okigbo shaped the post-independence canon through fiction, drama and poetry.
Adichie and Habila represent contemporary fiction’s turn to war, migration, dictatorship and oil politics.
Contemporary Nigerian poetry continues in print and online, often drawing on oral forms.

en.title: English Literature: Chaucer, Shakespeare and the Seventeenth Century
en.short: Covers Chaucer, Renaissance sonnet and lyric, Marlowe, Shakespeare, Milton, Metaphysical poets, epic and ode.

sections.heading: Medieval to Renaissance
sections.text:
Geoffrey Chaucer writes in Middle English before the period, but courses begin with him because he shows English poetry’s range: narrative, character and irony in The Canterbury Tales.

The Renaissance, a revival of classical learning, brought the sonnet from Italy and renewed lyric poetry. The Petrarchan sonnet has an octave and sestet; the English or Shakespearean sonnet has three quatrains and a couplet. Wyatt and Surrey adapted the form; Sidney, Spenser and Shakespeare developed it. A lyric is a short poem expressing a speaker’s feeling.

sections.heading: Stage and revenge
sections.text:
Marlowe’s blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, gave tragedy a powerful voice in Tamburlaine and Doctor Faustus. Shakespeare wrote comedies, histories, tragedies and sonnets.

The revenge tragedy, a play in which a wronged hero seeks vengeance, often ends in widespread death; Hamlet is the famous English example. Read a sonnet beside a scene: in Shakespeare’s Sonnet 18 the couplet closes the praise, while in Hamlet blank verse carries thought.

sections.heading: Milton, epic and ode
sections.text:
John Milton’s Paradise Lost is an epic, a long narrative poem on a grand scale with a heroic or cosmic subject. It was published after the civil war and Restoration, and its politics and theology are debated. Milton also wrote the ode 'On the Morning of Christ’s Nativity' and the pastoral elegy 'Lycidas'.

An ode is a formal lyric addressed to a person, object or idea. The Metaphysical poets, including John Donne, George Herbert and Andrew Marvell, use conceits, extended and surprising comparisons, and dramatic argument rather than smooth decoration.

sections.heading: Reformation and civil war
sections.text:
The English Reformation, the break from papal authority in the sixteenth century, made Bible translation, prayer book worship and religious argument central. Protestant writers valued plain style and inward conscience; Catholic and conformist voices also wrote.

The civil war and Commonwealth divided writers. Royalist poets celebrated order and loyalty; Parliamentarian and Puritan writers examined conscience and liberty. After 1660 the monarchy returned, and Milton’s epic looks back on lost hopes. Donne’s Holy Sonnets turn the sonnet into an argument with God, showing Reformation inwardness.

keyPoints: Chaucer’s Middle English poetry shows narrative range before the Renaissance.
The Petrarchan sonnet has an octave and sestet, while the English sonnet has three quatrains and a couplet.
Marlowe established blank verse as a powerful dramatic medium, and Hamlet is a revenge tragedy.
Milton’s Paradise Lost is an epic, and the ode is a formal lyric address.
Metaphysical poets use conceits and dramatic argument.
The Reformation and civil war shaped religious inwardness, political loyalty and Milton’s later epic.

en.title: English Literature: The Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries
en.short: The rise of the novel, Augustan satire, Romantic poetry, and Victorian fiction and verse.

sections.heading: The rise of the novel
sections.text: In England the novel took shape in the eighteenth century. Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe (1719) reads like a true account; Richardson’s Pamela (1740) is told in letters, an epistolary novel. Fielding replied with comic novels and a knowing narrator. Ian Watt, in The Rise of the Novel (1957), tied the form to a middle-class reading public, individualism and realistic detail. Austen worked on a smaller scale: Pride and Prejudice (1813) turns on courtship, property and judgement.

sections.heading: Augustan wit
sections.text: Augustan writers, named after the Rome of Emperor Augustus, admired classical order and polished the heroic couplet, a pair of rhyming lines in iambic pentameter. Pope used it in satire and in The Rape of the Lock; Swift attacked pride in Gulliver’s Travels (1726) and in A Modest Proposal (1729), a savage ironic pamphlet. Addison and Steele’s Spectator papers taught manners to a new urban readership. Wit here means verbal cleverness serving moral judgement.

sections.heading: The Romantic revolt
sections.text: Romantic writers trusted imagination and feeling over urban polish, and looked to nature, childhood and ordinary people. Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lyrical Ballads (1798), with Wordsworth’s Preface of 1800, became its manifesto; he called poetry the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, born of emotion recollected in tranquillity. The French Revolution of 1789 raised hopes that turned to disappointment. Keats’s odes of 1819 pursue beauty and mortality; his letters describe negative capability, the power to stay in uncertainties without reaching after fact and reason.

sections.heading: Victorians and empire
sections.text: Victorians faced industrialisation, reform and empire. Dickens serialised novels in monthly parts and attacked the courts in Bleak House (1852-53). Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847) and Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights (1847) used intense first-person and framed narration. Tennyson, poet laureate from 1850, mourned a friend in In Memoriam (1850). Edward Said, in Culture and Imperialism (1993), read such novels beside imperial wealth: Rochester’s fortune comes from the West Indies, and Mansfield Park depends on an Antiguan estate.

keyPoints: The eighteenth-century novel grew with a middle-class reading public and a claim to realistic detail.
Augustan poetry prized the heroic couplet, classical order and satiric wit.
Lyrical Ballads (1798) and its Preface of 1800 are the usual starting point for English Romanticism.
Keats’s negative capability names the power to remain in uncertainties without reaching after fact and reason.
Victorian novels were often serialised and took industrialisation, reform and empire as subjects.
Critics such as Said read nineteenth-century fiction alongside Britain’s imperial wealth.

en.title: English Literature: The Twentieth Century and After
en.short: Modernism in Eliot, Woolf, Joyce and Beckett, then post-war and postcolonial writing in English.

sections.heading: Modernist experiment
sections.text:
Modernism is a label for writing from roughly the 1890s to the 1930s that broke with Victorian realism. It favoured experiment with form, time, voice and allusion (references to earlier texts and myths).

T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land (1922) is a poem of fragments and shifting speakers; it uses the 'mythic method', setting modern disorder against ancient myth. Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925) and James Joyce’s Ulysses (1922) use stream of consciousness, which tries to show the flow of a character’s thoughts. Joyce also parodies many prose styles. The result is a literature of the inner life and of broken certainties after the First World War.

sections.heading: Drama and aftermath
sections.text:
Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot (first performed 1953) belongs to what critics call the Theatre of the Absurd. Two tramps wait for a Godot who never comes; plot, character and language are reduced. The play asks what can be said when old beliefs fail.

Beckett wrote in French and English, and his spare style influenced later drama and fiction. After 1945, writers also mixed realism with fantasy, parody and political comment. This writing is often called postmodern, though the label is disputed.

sections.heading: Empire and canon
sections.text:
Postcolonial literature is writing from former colonies and from migrant communities. It examines empire, identity, language and displacement. The canon, the body of works treated as central, expanded.

Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) uses English while drawing on Igbo proverbs and oral storytelling; it answers colonial images of Africa. Jean Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) rewrites Jane Eyre from the Caribbean. Salman Rushdie’s Midnight’s Children (1981) uses magic realism, which mixes realistic detail with fantastic events, to tell Indian history. Migration brought Caribbean, African and South Asian writers into British publishing and university syllabuses.

keyPoints: Modernism broke with Victorian realism and experimented with form, voice and time.
Eliot’s The Waste Land uses fragmentation and allusion; Woolf and Joyce use stream of consciousness.
Beckett’s Waiting for Godot reduces plot and language to ask what remains when beliefs fail.
Postcolonial writing examines empire, migration, identity and the politics of language.
Achebe’s Things Fall Apart shows how English can be reshaped by African oral forms and proverbs.
The canon of English literature expanded to include writers from Africa, the Caribbean and South Asia.

en.title: Literary Theory and Criticism
en.short: Structuralism, deconstruction, Marxism, feminism, psychoanalysis, postcolonialism and ecocriticism in practice.

sections.heading: Theory as a lens
sections.text: Literary theory is a set of assumptions about how texts make meaning. A critic uses a theory as a lens, not a formula. Structuralism, after Ferdinand de Saussure, treats meaning as produced by differences within a system of signs. Claude Lévi-Strauss and Roland Barthes applied this to myths and popular culture. Post-structuralism doubts fixed meaning; Jacques Derrida’s deconstruction shows how a text undermines its own oppositions.

sections.heading: Five more approaches
sections.text: Marxist criticism, from Karl Marx through Antonio Gramsci and Louis Althusser, asks how class, ideology and hegemony shape texts. Feminist criticism, from Virginia Woolf and Simone de Beauvoir to Sandra Gilbert, Susan Gubar and Hélène Cixous, examines patriarchy and gender construction. Psychoanalytic criticism, from Sigmund Freud to Jacques Lacan, reads desire, repression and the unconscious. Postcolonial criticism, with Edward Said, Gayatri Spivak and Homi Bhabha, studies colonial representation, the subaltern and hybridity. Ecocriticism, associated with Cheryll Glotfelty and Lawrence Buell, examines nature, place and environmental imagination.

sections.heading: One text, many readings
sections.text: Take an invented text: 'The farmer sold his land to the bank. That night his daughter dreamed of a river.' A structuralist notes the land/money and nature/culture oppositions. A deconstructionist shows the bank depends on the land it replaces. A Marxist reads debt and commodification. A feminist asks why the daughter speaks only through dream. A psychoanalytic critic treats the river as unconscious desire. A postcolonial critic may see the bank as neocolonial power. An ecocritic mourns the lost river and land.

sections.heading: Writing the essay
sections.text: Choose one approach, define its key terms, and state your claim. Close-read quotations for evidence, not plot summary. Show how the theory explains what another reading misses, and acknowledge limits. For example, a feminist essay on the text might argue that the daughter’s dream exposes a voice excluded from the sale. End by linking the reading to the text’s wider context, without forcing the theory onto every detail.

keyPoints: Structuralism treats meaning as difference within sign systems; deconstruction shows meaning is unstable and deferred.
Marxist criticism links texts to class, ideology and hegemony.
Feminist criticism examines patriarchy and gender construction; psychoanalytic criticism reads unconscious desire and repression.
Postcolonial criticism studies colonial representation, the subaltern and hybridity; ecocriticism studies nature, place and environmental imagination.
A critical essay should choose one approach, define its terms and support its claim with close reading.
Different theories can produce different valid readings of the same text.

en.title: Comparative Literature and Genre Studies
en.short: Comparative literature, translation problems, and genre comparison across European and African traditions.

sections.heading: What comparison means
sections.text: Comparative literature studies texts across national, linguistic and cultural borders. It is not a simple list of similarities; it asks how works travel, are translated, received and valued. Methods include close reading in the original where possible, historical and cultural context, reception history, and translation studies. A comparison should state its basis: theme, form, period or function. Otherwise it becomes loose analogy.

sections.heading: Translation and power
sections.text: Translation is never a word-for-word transfer. Languages divide meaning differently; sound, rhythm, idiom and cultural reference may have no equivalent. The translator chooses between literal accuracy and readable style. These choices shape what readers think a foreign literature is. Translation also carries power: which languages are translated, by whom, and for whom. Compare translations, not only originals.

sections.heading: Epic across traditions
sections.text: Epic is a long narrative of heroic action, often with supernatural help and communal importance. European classical epics such as Homer’s Iliad are written texts, though they grew from oral tradition. The Mande epic of Sunjata is performed by jeliw (griots), with music and audience. A useful comparison asks who performs, how the hero is praised or blamed, and what the genre does in each society. Do not assume the European model is the standard.

sections.heading: Novel and drama
sections.text: The novel is often treated as a modern European genre, but long prose narratives exist elsewhere. Compare what is narrated, who speaks, and how print or oral performance shapes form. Drama is written for performance. Greek theatre and African masquerade and ritual theatre differ in space and audience, yet both use costume, gesture and communal occasion. Modern African playwrights such as Wole Soyinka write for both page and stage. Genre labels should be tested against the text.

keyPoints: Comparative literature compares texts across languages, cultures and periods, and studies how they travel and are received.
Translation involves choices and loss, especially of sound, idiom and cultural reference, and it shapes reception.
Genre is a set of conventions and expectations, not a fixed natural category.
Epic, novel and drama take different forms in European and African traditions, so compare function and performance, not only surface features.
A good comparison states its basis and avoids treating one tradition as the standard.

en.title: First and Second Language Acquisition
en.short: How children acquire a first language, and how second-language learners build interlanguage and make errors.

sections.heading: First language: two views
sections.text:
Behaviourists such as B. F. Skinner held that children learn language by imitation, repetition and reinforcement: a word that gets a response becomes a habit. This explains routines but not why children produce sentences they have never heard.

Nativists such as Noam Chomsky argued that children are born with Universal Grammar, innate principles, and a language acquisition device. They say the input is too poor to explain grammar, so an inborn capacity is needed.

sections.heading: Interaction and use
sections.text:
Interactionists stress that language grows in social exchange. Adults use child-directed speech, simplified and repetitive, and scaffold the child, supporting a little beyond the child’s current level. Jerome Bruner and Lev Vygotsky are cited.

Usage-based theorists such as Michael Tomasello argue that children build constructions, or form-meaning patterns, from frequent input. General cognitive abilities such as pattern finding do the work; a separate grammar module is not needed.

sections.heading: Second language learning
sections.text:
Second language acquisition is learning another language after the first, in a classroom, community or both. The first language can help through positive transfer, where a similar pattern works, or hinder through negative transfer. Age, motivation, input and instruction matter.

For example, Ade, a Yoruba speaker learning English, says “She go market”. Yoruba does not mark present-tense third-person -s, so transfer may explain part of the error. Error analysis would ask whether Ade has not yet learned the rule.

sections.heading: Errors and interlanguage
sections.text:
The contrastive analysis hypothesis, linked to Robert Lado, predicted that differences between the first and second language cause difficulty, while similarities help. It overpredicted: many learner errors are developmental, not caused by the first language.

Error analysis, associated with S. P. Corder, treats errors as systematic evidence of the learner’s current rules. It separates errors, which are consistent, from mistakes, which are slips. Interlanguage, from Larry Selinker, is the learner’s changing system between the first language and the target. It can fossilise, or stop developing.

keyPoints: Behaviourism explains language as imitation and reinforcement; nativism explains it as an innate Universal Grammar.
Interactionists stress social support and child-directed speech; usage-based theory stresses constructions learned from frequent input.
The contrastive analysis hypothesis predicted difficulty from first-language and second-language differences but overstated it.
Error analysis treats learner errors as systematic evidence of the learner’s rules.
Interlanguage is the learner’s own changing system between the first language and the target.
First-language transfer can help or hinder second-language learning, alongside age, motivation and input.

en.title: Sociolinguistics: Language in Society
en.short: Language variation, dialect, code-switching, diglossia and language choice in Nigeria and African literature.

sections.heading: Variation and community
sections.text:
Sociolinguistics studies how language changes with social context. A dialect is a rule-governed variety of a language, marked by region or social group; it is not a broken form of the standard. An idiolect is one person’s individual speech pattern. A speech community is a group that shares norms for using and interpreting language, not simply a group that speaks the same tongue.

Variation follows region, social class, gender, age and style. Style means adjusting speech to audience and formality. William Labov’s New York study showed that pronunciation of /r/ varied by store status and by how carefully assistants spoke. Gender and age patterns are statistical and context-dependent, not fixed rules.

sections.heading: Codes and functions
sections.text:
Code-switching is alternating between languages or varieties within a conversation or sentence. It can be situational, when the setting changes, or metaphorical, when a speaker signals a second identity. Diglossia, as described by Charles Ferguson in 1959, is a stable arrangement in which two varieties of one language divide functions: a high variety for formal writing and public speech, and a low variety for everyday talk. Joshua Fishman extended the idea to different languages.

Consider a student in Lagos. She speaks Yoruba with her grandmother, Nigerian English in a lecture, and Nigerian Pidgin with friends. Each choice fits a domain, a setting such as family, school or friendship, and signals belonging. No variety is inherently inferior; prestige comes from social evaluation.

sections.heading: Literature and choice
sections.text:
African writers choose among languages and varieties for effect. Chinua Achebe wrote in English but used Igbo words and proverbs to carry Igbo speech patterns into the novel. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o later chose Gikuyu for fiction, as a political and cultural decision. In dialogue, code-switching can show a character’s education, class or setting.

These choices shape the reader’s access and the text’s identity. A novel that mixes English and Pidgin may reach a wider audience while marking local life. Sociolinguistic reading asks not only what is said but why that variety was chosen.

keyPoints: Sociolinguistics studies how language varies with region, class, gender, age and style.
A dialect is a rule-governed variety, and an idiolect is one person’s speech pattern.
A speech community shares norms for language use, not just a common language.
Code-switching alternates languages or varieties; diglossia divides high and low functions.
In multilingual Nigeria, language choice depends on domain, audience and identity.
African writers use English, indigenous languages and code-switching to shape meaning and audience.

en.title: Pragmatics and Discourse Analysis
en.short: Deixis, speech acts, implicature, politeness, relevance, cohesion, turn-taking and genre.

sections.heading: Pragmatics in context
sections.text: Pragmatics studies meaning that depends on context. Deixis is context-bound pointing: person (I, you), place (here, there) and time (now, tomorrow). In the invented line “I will meet you here tomorrow,” those words need the situation to be understood. Speech act theory (Austin, Searle) says utterances do things: the locutionary act is what is said; the illocutionary act is the act performed, such as promising; the perlocutionary act is its effect on the hearer.

sections.heading: Implicature and politeness
sections.text: Grice’s cooperative principle and maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner explain implicature: suggested meaning not stated. If Ada asks “Is Chidi coming?” and Bola replies “His car is at the mechanic’s,” Bola implies probably not, perhaps by flouting relation. Politeness theory (Brown and Levinson) centres on face, a person’s public self-image. Positive politeness shows closeness; negative politeness avoids imposition. Relevance theory (Sperber and Wilson) says hearers seek the most relevant interpretation for the least processing effort.

sections.heading: Discourse beyond sentence
sections.text: Discourse analysis studies language in use above the sentence. Cohesion is visible linking: reference (he, it), substitution, ellipsis, conjunction and lexical cohesion. Coherence is the underlying sense that makes a text hold together; a text can be cohesive yet incoherent if its links do not fit. Turn-taking organises talk: speakers take turns, use adjacency pairs (question and answer), prefer agreement and repair trouble. Genre is a socially recognised text type, such as a letter, sermon or chat, with expected conventions.

sections.heading: Analysing a case
sections.text: Take an invented passage: “Ngozi: You are late. Emeka: The road was bad.” Cohesion links it through the pronoun “you” and the lexical link between “late” and “road”. Coherence depends on shared knowledge that bad roads cause delay. Emeka’s reply is an indirect account and an implicature. The turn-taking is a complaint followed by an account. The genre is everyday conversation, so short turns and shared context are expected. In a literary passage, the same tools show how dialogue builds character and conflict.

keyPoints: Pragmatics explains meaning that depends on context, not only on words.
Deixis covers person, place and time expressions whose referents change with context.
Speech act theory separates what is said, the act performed and its effect.
Gricean implicature is meaning suggested by following or flouting the cooperative maxims.
Politeness protects face, and relevance theory explains interpretation by contextual effects and processing effort.
Discourse analysis uses cohesion, coherence, turn-taking and genre to explain texts beyond the sentence.

en.title: Stylistics: The Language of Literature
en.short: How linguistic description supports literary reading: foregrounding, transitivity, modality, metaphor.

sections.heading: What stylistics does
sections.text:
Stylistics describes the language of a text in order to explain how it produces meaning and effect. It borrows the tools of linguistics, such as grammar, lexis, sound and discourse, and applies them to literary reading.

It does not replace interpretation. It makes the evidence for an interpretation explicit, so that another reader can check it.

sections.heading: Foregrounding and deviation
sections.text:
Foregrounding is the quality of standing out from the surrounding language, so that a feature draws attention and invites interpretation. Two common means are deviation, a departure from the expected norm, and parallelism, the repetition of a pattern with variation.

In Blake’s "The Tyger", "fearful symmetry" deviates by joining fear to order, and the repeated question is parallelism. Both make the poem’s doubt about creation audible.

sections.heading: Transitivity, modality and metaphor
sections.text:
Transitivity, from M. A. K. Halliday’s systemic functional linguistics, asks who does what to whom. It labels processes (material, mental, verbal, relational), the participants involved and the circumstances. Modality covers the words that mark possibility, certainty and obligation, such as may, must and perhaps.

Metaphor carries meaning across domains. Its tenor is the subject, and its vehicle is the image used to describe it.

sections.heading: Analysing two texts
sections.text:
Method: describe the feature, give the evidence, then interpret, and test a rival reading. Take an invented prose example: "The clerk stamped the form. The rain had stopped, or so it seemed. He might have gone home." The first clause is a material process with a clear actor and goal, presenting the clerk as agent. The hedge "or so it seemed" and the modal "might have" weaken certainty, so the passage moves from fact to doubt.

For the poem, note the falling trochaic beat and the string of questions. The questions, not answers, carry the argument.

keyPoints: Stylistics uses linguistic description to make literary interpretation explicit and checkable.
Foregrounding works through deviation from a norm and parallelism of pattern.
Transitivity analysis shows who acts, who is acted upon, and what is left unstated.
Modality marks degrees of certainty, possibility and obligation in a text.
In metaphor, the tenor is the subject and the vehicle is the image that carries it.
A stylistic analysis should quote the evidence, interpret it, and test a rival reading.

en.title: Composition, Rhetoric and Academic Writing
en.short: Essay structure, argument, summary, paraphrase, referencing and the appeals of ethos, pathos and logos.

sections.heading: Essay and paragraph
sections.text:
An academic essay usually has an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. The introduction states the question and a thesis: the main claim the essay will defend. Each body paragraph should develop one main idea. A topic sentence announces that idea; evidence and analysis follow; a closing sentence links onward.

Coherence is the logical order of ideas. Cohesion is the visible linking through pronouns, repeated key terms and transitions such as however and therefore. A paragraph that jumps between ideas loses the reader.

sections.heading: Argument and appeals
sections.text:
Argument means supporting a claim with reasons and evidence, not merely asserting an opinion. A strong argument anticipates a counterargument and answers it.

Rhetoric, the art of persuasion, uses three classical appeals. Ethos is the writer’s credibility, built by fair tone, accurate citation and clear expertise. Pathos is appeal to emotion, used honestly and sparingly. Logos is appeal to reasoning and evidence. For example, a student arguing for longer library hours might cite usage figures, answer the objection about cost, and keep a calm tone.

sections.heading: Summary and sources
sections.text:
To summarise, state the main ideas in fewer words and in your own sentence structure. A paraphrase restates a passage in your own words while keeping its meaning, and it still needs a citation. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words or ideas as your own. It includes copied text, unacknowledged paraphrase and, in many institutions, submitting your own earlier work again.

Referencing gives credit and lets readers check sources. In-text citations and a reference list must follow your department’s style, such as APA, MLA or Harvard; check the current guide.

sections.heading: Exams, reports, publication
sections.text:
Examination answers need a quick plan: read the question, note the command word, allot time by marks, and state a clear thesis. Reports for employers or agencies are structured for action: headings, findings, conclusions and recommendations.

Publication follows the journal’s guidelines, including abstract, length, referencing and peer review. Edit for accuracy and keep a record of sources as you work.

keyPoints: An essay needs a clear thesis, body paragraphs with one main idea each, and a conclusion that follows the argument.
Coherence is logical order; cohesion is visible linking through transitions, pronouns and repeated terms.
A strong argument supports a claim with evidence and answers a counterargument.
Ethos is credibility, pathos is emotion and logos is reasoning and evidence.
Paraphrase and summary use your own words but still need citations; unacknowledged borrowing is plagiarism.
Follow your department’s current referencing style and the journal’s guidelines when publishing.

en.title: Literature and Society: Politics, Gender and the Environment
en.short: Postcolonial, feminist and ecocritical readings of African texts, censorship and representation.

sections.heading: Reading for power
sections.text: A postcolonial reading asks how literature and criticism carry the history of empire. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) argued that Western writing about the East built a picture that helped justify colonial rule. Gayatri Spivak’s "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988) asks whether the powerless can be heard, or only through others’ words. Chinua Achebe’s "An Image of Africa" (1977) reads Conrad’s Heart of Darkness as reducing Africans to background. A Marxist reading adds class: who owns, who labours, who speaks.

sections.heading: Gender and feminist readings
sections.text: Feminist criticism asks how a text imagines women’s lives, work and speech, and who narrates. Buchi Emecheta’s The Joys of Motherhood (1979) shows motherhood in colonial Lagos as both honour and trap for Nnu Ego. Mariama Bâ’s So Long a Letter (1979; English 1981) uses letters from a Senegalese widow to examine marriage, polygamy and girls’ schooling. African feminists do not simply copy Western feminism: colonial and local histories shaped gender differently, so analysis must begin from African conditions.

sections.heading: Environment and ecocriticism
sections.text: Ecocriticism reads how literature imagines land, water, animals and human use of them; the term is usually traced to William Rueckert (1978). In African writing land is often both livelihood and dispossession. Ken Saro-Wiwa, Nigerian writer and Ogoni campaigner, wrote fiction and led protest against oil pollution in Ogoniland; he was executed in 1995. Ben Okri’s The Famished Road (1991) gives road and forest a living presence through its spirit child narrator.

sections.heading: Censorship and responsibility
sections.text: Censorship is control of what may be published or performed. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o co-wrote the Gikuyu play Ngaahika Ndeenda (I Will Marry When I Want, 1977) with Ngũgĩ wa Mirii; performed at Kamĩrĩthũ, it led to his detention. His Decolonising the Mind (1986) argued for writing in African languages. The ethics of representation asks who may tell whose story. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s talk "The Danger of a Single Story" (2009) warns against reducing a people to one narrative. Censorship law differs by country; check it.

keyPoints: A postcolonial reading asks how texts and criticism carry the history of empire.
Said’s Orientalism (1978) and Spivak’s "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988) are founding statements of postcolonial criticism.
Feminist criticism asks who narrates and how texts imagine women’s lives; African feminists insist on starting from African conditions.
Ecocriticism reads how literature imagines land, water and animals, and it links to environmental justice.
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o's detention after Ngaahika Ndeenda (1977) shows how censorship works in practice.
The ethics of representation asks who may tell whose story, and warns against the single story.

en.title: Research Methods and the Long Essay
en.short: Framing questions, reviewing sources, theory, citation and writing the long essay.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A research question is the precise problem your essay answers. It should be narrow enough for the word limit and open enough to need evidence. Amina, a student in Lagos, begins with “Nigerian novels and the city” and narrows it to “How do two Nigerian novels portray city life?” She states a thesis, the answer she will argue, not merely the topic. A good question names the texts, period or issue, and angle. Check that the department has approved the scope.

sections.heading: Sources and notes
sections.text: Primary sources are the works or evidence you analyse: novels, poems, plays, manuscripts, interviews or archival records. Secondary sources are other people’s interpretations, such as journal articles, book chapters and reviews. Search the library catalogue for books and subject databases for articles; use the internet for leads, then verify. Keep a working bibliography early. For every note, record author, title, year, page number and whether the words are a quotation or your paraphrase. This prevents plagiarism, presenting another’s words or ideas as your own.
