sections.heading: Theory and citation
sections.text: A theoretical approach is the lens you use to interpret evidence, such as formalism, feminism or postcolonial criticism. Choose one that helps answer the question, and explain its key terms; do not simply list theories. Citation styles differ. MLA (Modern Language Association) is common in literary studies and APA (American Psychological Association) in language and education, but follow your department. Cite quotations and ideas, and include a works cited or reference list. Quote exactly, use page numbers, and keep quotations short.

sections.heading: Structure and supervision
sections.text: Most long essays have an introduction with the question and thesis, a literature review that groups scholarship by issue, a methods or approach section, analytical chapters, a conclusion and references. Requirements vary by country and institution; check the handbook for length, format and deadlines. A supervisor advises on scope, sources and drafts; the student researches and writes. Agree a schedule, submit drafts on time, and record meetings. Seek ethical approval before interviews.

keyPoints: A research question should be narrow, answerable and supported by a thesis.
Primary sources are the texts or evidence you analyse; secondary sources interpret them.
Keep full bibliographic details and page numbers for every note to avoid plagiarism.
Choose a theoretical approach that helps answer the question and explain its terms.
MLA is common in literature and APA in language study, but follow your department’s style.
The supervisor advises; the student plans, researches, drafts and submits on time.

en.title: Advanced Literary Theory and Philosophy of Criticism
en.short: Affect theory, new materialism, world literature, translation studies and canon debates.

sections.heading: Criticism as philosophy
sections.text: Philosophy of criticism asks what criticism is for: description, interpretation, evaluation or political diagnosis. It also asks what counts as evidence and who a reading serves. Close reading means attending to a text’s own words, images and structure, not relying on summaries. Ask what an approach explains, hides, and what would count against it. Postcritique, associated with Rita Felski, asks whether critique has become a habit. Test that claim by reading Felski beside a text she discusses.

sections.heading: Affect and matter
sections.text: Affect theory studies bodily intensities and feelings that precede or exceed conscious emotion and language. It can illuminate tone, atmosphere and reader response, but its evidence is often interpretive and hard to verify. New materialism treats matter as active and refuses a sharp split between nature and culture. Jane Bennett’s Vibrant Matter (2010) is a common starting point. Its limit is that agency can become so widely distributed that human responsibility blurs.

sections.heading: World literature and translation
sections.text: World literature is literature that circulates beyond its language and nation. David Damrosch treats a work as world literature when it gains in translation; Franco Moretti proposes distant reading, using patterns rather than close reading. World Anglophone studies examines English-language writing beyond Britain and the United States, shaped by empire and global markets. Translation studies treats translation as interpretation and power; Lawrence Venuti contrasts domestication, making a text smooth for the target reader, with foreignization, marking its difference. A seminar can compare two translations of one passage from Achebe’s Things Fall Apart to show what shifts in idiom, address and cultural reference. Limits: world literature can privilege English and the market, and the domestication/foreignization pair can oversimplify.

sections.heading: Canon and limits
sections.text: Canon debates concern which texts are taught, valued and printed. Harold Bloom defends aesthetic excellence in The Western Canon (1994); John Guillory asks how schools distribute cultural capital, the valued knowledge and credentials they pass on. Both views matter: value is real, but institutions select it. The student’s task is to judge each approach by its evidence and its blind spots.

keyPoints: Philosophy of criticism asks what criticism does, what counts as evidence and whom a reading serves.
Affect theory studies intensities beyond conscious emotion, but its evidence is often interpretive.
New materialism treats matter as active and tests the nature/culture split, yet can blur responsibility.
World literature and world Anglophone studies examine circulation, translation and power, not just texts.
Translation is interpretation; Venuti’s domestication and foreignization name two strategies with limits.
Canon debates are about value and institutional selection; read Bloom and Guillory together.

en.title: Advanced English Linguistics and Corpus Methods
en.short: Advanced phonology, syntax, semantics, corpus building, frequency and collocation analysis.

sections.heading: Theory and interfaces
sections.text:
Advanced linguistics links sound, structure and meaning. Phonology studies contrastive features, syllables, stress and tone, and constraint-based accounts such as Optimality Theory, which ranks competing constraints.

Syntax models constituency, phrase structure, agreement and movement; formal grammars make precise predictions. Semantics studies compositionality, truth conditions, lexical relations and event structure. These theories generate hypotheses that corpus data can test, but a corpus shows usage, not a speaker’s full competence.

sections.heading: Building a corpus
sections.text:
A corpus is a principled, machine-readable collection of texts. Design begins with the research question, then sampling, balance, representativeness, size and metadata such as region, age, gender, education and text type.

For African Englishes, record spoken and written data across settings and mark the variety. Annotation adds part-of-speech tags, lemmas or syntax. Concordancers such as AntConc and Sketch Engine help search, but copyright and consent must be respected.

sections.heading: Queries and measures
sections.text:
A concordance lists a node word, the word you search for, with its context. Raw frequency is a count; normalised frequency allows comparison. The formula is raw count ÷ corpus size × 1,000,000. If "abeg" occurs 240 times in a 4,000,000-word corpus, its frequency is 240 ÷ 4,000,000 × 1,000,000 = 60 per million.

Collocation is co-occurrence within a window, often five words left and right. Compare observed co-occurrence with chance; mutual information and log-likelihood are common measures. High mutual information favours rare pairs, so report raw counts too.

sections.heading: Reporting findings
sections.text:
Report the corpus design, size, sources, annotation, tools and query. Give raw and normalised figures, the statistical test and its effect size. Distinguish a frequent pattern from a significant one.

For African Englishes, compare with a suitable reference corpus and name the variety. A small or unbalanced corpus supports limited claims. State limitations and make queries reproducible.

keyPoints: A corpus is a principled, machine-readable sample of language, and its design must match the research question.
Normalised frequency is raw count ÷ corpus size × 1,000,000, which allows comparison across corpora of different sizes.
A concordance shows a node word in context, while collocation measures co-occurrence within a stated window.
Collocation statistics compare observed co-occurrence with chance, and high mutual information can favour rare pairs.
Corpus findings should report design, annotation, tools, raw and normalised counts, tests and limitations.
African Englishes need corpora that record variety, region, speaker and text type, and comparisons must name the reference corpus.

en.title: Research Design and Dissertation in English Studies
en.short: Narrowing a topic, proposals, archives, evidence, ethics, supervision, writing up and oral defence.

sections.heading: From topic to proposal
sections.text: A dissertation is an original, supervised study. Narrow a broad interest into a research question answerable with available texts and time. A proposal is a short plan: it states the question, why it matters, the primary texts or data, the method, a chapter outline and a timetable. A workable question is focused: not 'Nigerian poetry' but 'how a named poet’s later collection uses oral forms', an invented example. Check sources exist before committing. Primary sources are works or documents studied directly; secondary sources are other scholars’ interpretations.

sections.heading: Archives and evidence
sections.text: Archives hold unpublished or rare material: letters, drafts, manuscripts, newspapers, recordings. A manuscript is a handwritten or typed text, often a draft. Plan visits, check catalogues and permissions, and record reference codes and dates exactly. Combine close reading, careful analysis of language and form in a short passage, with linguistic or historical evidence. For example, count pronoun use across a small corpus, a collected body of texts, then read key passages closely. Historical evidence might be publication dates, censorship records or readers’ letters. Triangulation means using more than one kind of evidence to support a claim.

sections.heading: Ethics and supervision
sections.text: Research ethics covers honesty, consent, confidentiality and copyright. Quote accurately, cite every source, and do not fabricate evidence. For interviews or personal papers, obtain informed consent: explain the study and the person’s right to withdraw. Supervision is a working partnership. Bring written work and specific questions to meetings, agree a schedule, and keep a record of advice. Ask early about the department’s rules on word length, formatting and submission; these vary by university and country.

sections.heading: Writing up and defence
sections.text: Write in stages: chapter plan, drafts, revisions, final edit. Keep a research log of decisions and sources. The oral defence, or viva, is a meeting where examiners question you. Prepare a short account of your question, method and contribution. Anticipate weaknesses. In the defence, answer directly, admit limits, and distinguish evidence from speculation. Check your institution’s regulations for format and timing.

keyPoints: A dissertation proposal states a focused research question, its significance, primary sources or data, method, chapter outline and timetable.
Primary sources are studied directly; secondary sources are other scholars’ interpretations.
Archives and manuscripts require careful planning, exact references and permission checks.
Combine close reading with linguistic or historical evidence, and use triangulation to strengthen claims.
Research ethics require honesty, accurate citation, informed consent and respect for copyright.
Supervision works best with written drafts, specific questions, agreed schedules and records of advice; prepare for the oral defence by knowing your method and limits.

en.title: Frontier Areas: Digital Humanities and Global Anglophone Studies
en.short: Digital humanities methods and global anglophone debates, with African literature examples.

sections.heading: Digital humanities
sections.text: Digital humanities (DH) uses computing to study texts and culture. It includes making digital editions, building archives, analysing corpora and visualising data. DH is not only a set of tools. It changes what counts as evidence, because a claim can be tested against a whole collection rather than a few close-read passages. It also raises questions about access, labour and who owns the archive.

sections.heading: Encoding and distant reading
sections.text: Text encoding marks up a text with tags that describe structure and meaning. The Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) is a common standard for this, written in XML, a markup language. A student might encode an African praise poem, tagging speaker, place, refrain and translation. Distant reading, a term linked to Franco Moretti, studies large collections by counting features such as titles, genres or words instead of reading every text closely. Suppose a corpus (a collection of texts) of 50 novels has 20 by African writers. They are 20 ÷ 50 = 40% of the sample. That figure describes the corpus, not literature as a whole.

sections.heading: Mapping and archives
sections.text: Mapping plots places named in texts onto maps. It can show how a novel imagines Lagos, London or the Atlantic world, and where characters move. Digital archives make rare magazines, oral recordings and manuscripts searchable, but scans can be poor and metadata (data about the files) thin. A researcher must ask who was digitised and who was left out.

sections.heading: Global anglophone debates
sections.text: Global anglophone studies examines literature written in English across the world. It overlaps with postcolonial studies, which analyses empire, race, language and resistance. Debates ask whether 'anglophone' hides the power of English, whether national labels such as Nigerian literature still help, and how to decolonise reading lists. Digital methods can support these debates, but they do not settle them. Counting cannot replace interpretation; it can only point to patterns that close reading must explain.

keyPoints: Digital humanities uses computing to create, analyse and share texts and cultural records.
Text encoding with TEI uses XML tags to describe a text’s structure and meaning.
Distant reading studies patterns across large corpora rather than interpreting single texts closely.
Literary mapping plots places and movement in texts and archives.
Global anglophone studies examines English-language literature worldwide and overlaps with postcolonial studies.
Digital methods raise questions about access, labour and archive selection, and they support but do not replace close reading.
